claims.text: Rapid solidification creates a supersaturated matrix in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Modest thermal or environmental aging causes localized spinodal decomposition of the supersaturated matrix.
The proposed decomposition forms fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Formation of Mg-rich precipitates sequesters Mg from the surrounding matrix.
Sequestering Mg in precipitates reduces galvanic coupling between Mg and more electronegative constituents.
Reduced galvanic coupling lowers localized corrosion rates.
The microstructural evolution promotes a more uniform and adherent protective oxide layer at high temperature.
The initial alloy contains a supersaturated solid solution and a heterogeneous microstructure.
Mild aging can permit phase separation without bringing the alloy to full equilibrium.
Fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates alter local galvanic interactions.
Fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates alter oxide-formation dynamics.
Aging at approximately 300–400°C will produce a statistically significant population of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the as-cast state.
The aged alloy will have a lower localized corrosion rate than the initial as-cast alloy.
The aged alloy will have better oxidation resistance at approximately 700°C than the initial as-cast alloy.
Improved oxidation resistance will coincide with a more uniform and adherent oxide layer.
The proposed pathway applies to Mg-containing alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ in which constituent-property differences promote intermetallic formation.
Compositions outside the stated design range may not follow the proposed evolution pathway.
